title: The Filipino-American War
subtitle: It started two days before the treaty was ratified, and lasted three years.
objectives: Describe how the war began in February 1899
Explain why Aguinaldo switched to guerrilla warfare
Describe the stand at Tirad Pass
Describe the capture of Aguinaldo and the end of the war
Explain the human cost of the war

cards.title: One shot on a bridge, and everything followed
cards.text: On the evening of 4 February 1899, an American sentry shot a Filipino soldier at San Juan. By morning it was a war.

cards.title: February 1899 to July 1902
cards.text: Tap through. Several quiz questions come from these dates.

cards.title: Two days later the treaty was ratified
cards.text: The US Senate had been arguing about whether to keep the Philippines at all. The vote came on 6 February, two days after the shooting.
points: **It passed by one vote** more than the required margin.
**News of fighting** reached Washington first.
**Historians still argue** about how much that mattered.
**The timing is a fact.** The cause is a debate.

cards.title: Crash investigators never look for one cause
cards.text: Almost no accident has a single cause. It is a chain, and removing any one link stops it.
points: **Tenerife, 1977:** two radio calls overlapped.
**Fog, a delay, a full fuel load**, all at once.
**Pull out any one link** and 583 people live.
**Ask the same of February 1899.**

question.text: When did the Filipino-American War begin?
question.explain: 4 February 1899, at San Juan bridge. The Senate ratified the treaty two days later.

cards.title: A conventional war they could not win
cards.text: For nine months the Filipino army fought in the open, in lines, against better-armed and better-supplied troops. It went badly.
points: **They lost Manila within days.**
**They lost Malolos in March 1899.**
**Standing and fighting** played to American strengths.
**By November the regular army was finished.**

cards.title: You do not keep boxing somebody who is bigger
cards.text: If the straight fight is going badly, you change the fight. Aguinaldo dissolved the regular army and switched to guerrilla warfare.
points: **November 1899**, at Bayambang in Pangasinan.
**Small units, ambushes, no fixed lines.**
**It cost the Americans far more** and lasted years.
**Changing style** is not the same as giving up.

question.text: Why did Aguinaldo switch to guerrilla warfare?
options: Conventional battles played to American strengths
He had run out of soldiers entirely
It was the only style Filipinos knew
question.explain: Better-armed troops win open battles. Ambush and dispersal took away that advantage.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Part 2 is Tirad Pass, the capture, and the cost. Some of it is hard. Your place is saved.

cards.title: A narrow pass in the mountains of Ilocos Sur
cards.text: By December 1899 Aguinaldo was being hunted north. Sixty men stayed behind at Tirad Pass to buy him time.

cards.title: Gregorio del Pilar
cards.text: He was twenty-four years old and already a general. He chose the pass because it was narrow enough for sixty men to hold.
points: **They held it for around five hours.**
**An American unit found a way round** the side.
**Del Pilar was killed** in the fighting.
**Aguinaldo escaped.** The delay worked.

cards.title: A chokepoint is a real military idea
cards.text: Narrow ground cancels a numbers advantage, because only so many people can come through at once. That is why he chose the pass.
points: **Sixty men cannot beat an army in the open.**
**In a gap two metres wide**, numbers matter less.
**It works until somebody finds a flank.**
**Somebody did.**

question.text: Why did Gregorio del Pilar make his stand at Tirad Pass?
options: It was narrow enough that a small force could hold it
It was the only road in the country
He had been ordered to attack there
question.explain: Narrow ground cancels a numbers advantage. Sixty men held it for hours, and Aguinaldo got away.

cards.title: The capture at Palanan
cards.text: American officers reached Aguinaldo's camp in Isabela by disguising themselves as prisoners of a friendly Filipino unit.
points: **Palanan, Isabela**, 23 March 1901.
**He swore allegiance to the United States** days later.
**He called on others to stop fighting.**
**Many of them did not.**

cards.title: The part the dates do not show
cards.text: Around 4,200 American soldiers died. Around 20,000 Filipino fighters died. Far more civilians died than either.
points: **Estimates of civilian deaths start at 200,000.**
**Most were from famine and disease**, not battle.
**Whole areas were emptied** and villages burned.
**Samar in 1901** was the worst of it.

cards.title: For a long time it was not called a war
cards.text: In American writing it was the Philippine Insurrection for most of a century. An insurrection is a rebellion against a legitimate government.
points: **Calling it that settles the argument** in advance.
**A war is between two sides.**
**An insurrection has only one legitimate side.**
**One word, and the whole story changes.**

question.text: More civilians died in the war than soldiers on either side.
question.explain: True, by a very long way. Most died of famine and disease rather than in fighting.

terms.def: Where the first shot was fired, on 4 February 1899.
Small units, ambushes and no fixed lines. Adopted in November 1899.
2 December 1899. Del Pilar and 60 men held it so Aguinaldo could escape.
The general who died at Tirad Pass, aged 24.
The town in Isabela where Aguinaldo was captured in March 1901.
The old American name for the war. The word chooses a side.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **4 February 1899.** The treaty was ratified two days later.
**November 1899:** the war goes guerrilla.
**Tirad Pass, December 1899.** Del Pilar was 24.
**The civilian cost** was greater than both armies combined.

quiz.text: Where and when did the war begin?
quiz.explain: An American sentry shot a Filipino soldier on the evening of 4 February 1899.
quiz.objective: Describe how the war began in February 1899

quiz.text: What happened two days after the first shot?
options: The US Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris
quiz.explain: 6 February 1899. Historians still argue about how much the fighting influenced that vote.
quiz.objective: Describe how the war began in February 1899

quiz.text: Why did conventional battles go badly for the Filipino army?
options: Open battle favoured the better-armed and better-supplied side
quiz.explain: Standing and fighting in lines played directly to American strengths.
quiz.objective: Explain why Aguinaldo switched to guerrilla warfare

quiz.text: When did Aguinaldo switch to guerrilla warfare?
quiz.explain: At Bayambang in Pangasinan, he dissolved the regular army. The war then lasted years longer.
quiz.objective: Explain why Aguinaldo switched to guerrilla warfare

quiz.text: Who commanded the stand at Tirad Pass?
quiz.explain: Del Pilar, aged 24. He was killed holding the pass so Aguinaldo could escape north.
quiz.objective: Describe the stand at Tirad Pass

quiz.text: What was the purpose of the stand at Tirad Pass?
options: To delay the Americans so Aguinaldo could escape
quiz.explain: Sixty men on narrow ground, holding for hours. The delay worked and Aguinaldo got away.
quiz.objective: Describe the stand at Tirad Pass

quiz.text: Gregorio del Pilar survived Tirad Pass.
quiz.explain: False. He was killed in the fighting, at twenty-four years old.
quiz.objective: Describe the stand at Tirad Pass

quiz.explain: 23 March 1901. American officers reached his camp disguised as prisoners.
quiz.objective: Describe the capture of Aguinaldo and the end of the war

quiz.text: What did Aguinaldo do after his capture?
options: He swore allegiance to the United States and called for an end to fighting
He escaped and continued the war
quiz.explain: He swore allegiance within days. Many commanders kept fighting regardless.
quiz.objective: Describe the capture of Aguinaldo and the end of the war

quiz.text: When was the war officially declared over?
quiz.explain: 4 July 1902, though Malvar had surrendered in April and fighting continued in some regions.
quiz.objective: Describe the capture of Aguinaldo and the end of the war

quiz.text: Most of the Filipino deaths in the war were soldiers killed in battle.
quiz.explain: False. Civilian deaths, mostly from famine and disease, far outnumbered combatant deaths.
quiz.objective: Explain the human cost of the war

quiz.text: Why does it matter that Americans long called it the Philippine Insurrection?
options: An insurrection has only one legitimate side, so the word settles the argument
It was the official Filipino name too
It made the war sound longer
quiz.explain: A war is between two sides. An insurrection is a rebellion against a legitimate government.
quiz.objective: Explain the human cost of the war

teacher.summary: Week 7 Social Studies covers the Filipino-American War, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is the hardest topic of the term and the lesson does not soften it: the civilian death toll is stated, it is put alongside the military figures so the scale is visible, and the causes are named as famine and disease rather than battle. The naming card is deliberately included — 'Philippine Insurrection' was the standard American term for most of a century, and noticing that one word decides who is legitimate is a transferable historical skill. The chokepoint card explains why sixty men at Tirad Pass was a rational military decision rather than a suicidal gesture, which is how it is usually told.
discussion: Ask why the timing of the Senate vote matters. Two days is a fact; the causal link is a real historical argument.
Ask why changing to guerrilla war was a strategic decision rather than a retreat.
Ask what narrow ground does to a numbers advantage. Tirad Pass makes sense once that lands.
Ask what changes when you call something an insurrection rather than a war.
teacher.extension: Have him write two one-paragraph accounts of February 1899, one for an American newspaper and one for a Malolos one. Neither has to lie for them to be irreconcilable.
misconceptions: 'The war started because of the Treaty of Paris.' The first shot came two days before the Senate ratified it.
'Guerrilla war was a sign of collapse.' It was a deliberate change of strategy, and it made the war last years longer.
'The war ended when Aguinaldo was captured.' Fighting continued. It was declared over in July 1902 and went on in places after that.
'Most deaths were soldiers.' Civilian deaths from famine and disease were many times higher.
